topics.title: Meaning of development: growth, maturation and development

learn.hook: Your baby cousin goes from lying flat to crawling to running around the wedding hall in barely two years. Your grandparents keep changing too, in wisdom, patience and health. Development never really stops.
points: Development is the pattern of progressive, orderly and predictable changes that begin at conception and continue throughout life, until death.

Growth: increase in the size of the body or its parts (height, weight). Maturation: changes that follow an orderly sequence largely set by the genetic plan (e.g. walking emerges when the body is ready).
Development is broader: it includes growth and maturation but also changes in thinking, emotions and social relationships brought about by experience.
Development involves three interacting processes: biological (physical changes), cognitive (thought, intelligence, language) and socio-emotional (emotions, personality, relationships).

example.q: Classify: (a) Arjun grows 6 cm taller in a year. (b) A baby starts walking at about the same age as most babies, whatever the training. (c) A teenager learns to manage anger and make friends.
steps: (a) Increase in size = growth.
(b) Change following a genetic timetable = maturation.
(c) Change in emotions and relationships through experience = socio-emotional development.

learn.hook: A 75-year-old learning to use UPI to pay her vegetable vendor is still developing. The life-span view says no age is 'finished': we gain and lose abilities at every stage.
points: Development is lifelong: no single age period dominates; every stage from infancy to old age matters.
Development is multi-dimensional (biological, cognitive, socio-emotional) and multi-directional: some abilities increase while others decrease (e.g. older adults gain wisdom but may lose speed).
Development is highly plastic: abilities can be modified by experience at any age, e.g. memory can improve with training even in old age.
Development is influenced by historical conditions: those growing up during the Emergency, the 1991 reforms or the COVID-19 pandemic had different experiences.
Development is studied by many disciplines (psychology, sociology, biology, medicine…) and is contextual: it happens in a setting of heredity, environment, culture and family.

steps: The difference is due to the time period in which they grew up.

example.answer: Development is influenced by historical conditions.

learn.hook: Two seeds of the same mango variety are planted, one in rich soil with water, the other in a dry patch. The genes are identical; the harvest isn't. Human development works much the same way.
points: Heredity: characteristics passed from parents to children through genes. Genotype = a person's genetic heritage (the genes); phenotype = the observable characteristics (height, eye colour, personality traits) that result.
Environment: the physical and social surroundings (nutrition, family, school, culture) in which a person develops.
Nature and nurture interact: development is the product of both, not of either alone.
Genes set a range within which a trait can develop; the environment determines where in that range a person ends up (e.g. a child with genes for tallness may stay short with poor nutrition).
Some traits (e.g. eye colour) are strongly shaped by genes; others (e.g. language spoken, values) are much more open to environmental influence.

example.q: Identical twins (same genes) are raised apart, one with good nutrition and schooling, the other with poor nutrition. As adults, the first is taller and scores higher on tests. Explain using genotype and phenotype.
steps: Same genes → same genotype.

Genes set a possible range; the environment decided where each twin ended up within it.
example.answer: Same genotype, different phenotypes, because the environment works within the range genes allow.

learn.hook: A child's school marks can drop because her father's factory shifted him to night shifts. She never set foot in that factory, yet it shaped her life. Bronfenbrenner's model explains how.
points: Urie Bronfenbrenner described the environment as five nested systems around the child.

Microsystem: the immediate settings the child directly interacts with (family, school, peers, neighbourhood). Mesosystem: relations between microsystems (e.g. parent-teacher meetings, family-peer links).
Exosystem: settings the child is not directly part of but which affect the child (e.g. a parent's workplace, local government decisions).
Macrosystem: the broader culture, values, customs and laws of the society.
Chronosystem: events and transitions over time in the child's life and in society (e.g. parents' divorce, shift to digital schooling, or the death of a grandparent).

example.q: Place each in Bronfenbrenner's systems: (a) Rohit's mother's office cuts salaries; (b) Rohit's teacher and parents meet monthly; (c) Indian cultural respect for elders; (d) Rohit's family moves cities when he is 10.
steps: (a) Affects Rohit through his mother; he isn't part of the office → exosystem.
(b) Link between two microsystems → mesosystem.
(c) Wider culture and values → macrosystem.
(d) A life transition over time → chronosystem.

learn.reallife: The Right to Education Act (a macrosystem/exosystem influence) changed which school millions of children attend, which then changed their peers and teachers (their microsystem).

topics.title: Sinha's ecological model, culture and developmental stages

learn.hook: An Indian child's world isn't just home and school; it is also a crowded joint family, the neighbourhood chai shop and the family's social and economic position. Durganand Sinha built a model for exactly this.
points: Durganand Sinha's ecological model of the development of the Indian child pictures the environment as two concentric layers.
The upper, most visible layer: home, school and peer group, which the child directly experiences.
The surrounding layer: the wider social and physical conditions such as the family's social and economic status, crowding and availability of facilities; the two layers interact and change over time.
Culture shapes developmental goals and parenting: for example, many Indian families value interdependence and respect for elders, while some other cultures stress early independence.
Developmental stages (prenatal, infancy, childhood, adolescence, adulthood, old age) each come with developmental tasks: skills and behaviour patterns a society expects at that stage.

example.q: Which layer of Sinha's model? (a) Riya's peer group at school; (b) her family living in a one-room house in a crowded area.
steps: (a) Peer group is directly experienced → upper (visible) layer.
(b) Crowding and living conditions are wider conditions → surrounding layer.

learn.reallife: In many Indian homes grandparents help raise children, which reflects a cultural macro-goal of interdependence; developmental psychologists in India study how this shapes children's social skills.

learn.hook: For about nine months before you were born, you were already developing at astonishing speed, and your mother's diet, health and stress were part of the story.
points: The prenatal period runs from conception to birth (about nine months). It has three periods: germinal (about the first two weeks), embryonic (about 2 to 8 weeks, when major organs form) and fetal (from about 2 months until birth).
Teratogens are environmental agents that can cause birth defects: maternal diseases (e.g. rubella/German measles, HIV/AIDS), drugs, alcohol, tobacco, radiation and pollution.

topics.title: Infancy: reflexes, motor and sensory development

learn.hook: Stroke a newborn's cheek and she turns her head and opens her mouth. Nobody taught her that. Newborns arrive pre-loaded with survival reflexes.
points: Reflexes are automatic, unlearned responses with survival value: rooting (turns head and opens mouth when cheek is touched), sucking (sucks object placed in mouth), Moro (startle: throws arms outward at a sudden loud noise or loss of support), Babinski (toes fan out when the sole is stroked), grasping (grips an object placed in the palm), blinking (closes eyes to bright light or puff of air).
Motor development follows milestones: rolling over, sitting, crawling, standing, walking.
Cephalocaudal trend: development proceeds from head to foot (head control comes before walking). Proximodistal trend: from the centre of the body outwards (arm control before finger control).
Newborns can see (vision is blurry at first), hear (they recognise the mother's voice), smell (recognise the mother's smell), taste (prefer sweet) and are sensitive to touch and pain.

example.q: A baby can hold her head up at 2 months, sit at about 6 months and walk at around a year. She can wave her whole arm long before she can pick up a raisin with thumb and finger. Name the two trends.
steps: Head control → sitting → walking: top to bottom → cephalocaudal.
Arm control before finger control: centre to periphery → proximodistal.

topics.title: Infancy: sensorimotor thought, attachment and temperament

learn.hook: Hide a toy under a dupatta in front of a 4-month-old and she stops looking for it, as if it has vanished. A year-old baby lifts the cloth. Something big has happened in her mind.
points: Piaget's sensorimotor stage (birth to about 2 years): infants understand the world through senses and actions (looking, grasping, sucking). A key achievement is object permanence, knowing that objects continue to exist when out of sight.

Attachment is the close emotional bond between the infant and the caregiver. Harlow's study: infant monkeys clung to a soft cloth 'mother' rather than a wire 'mother' that gave milk, which shows the importance of contact comfort, not just feeding.
Securely attached infants use the caregiver as a safe base to explore; insecurely attached infants may avoid the caregiver or show anxious, clingy behaviour.
Erikson's first stage, trust vs mistrust: warm, consistent care builds a sense of trust; neglect or inconsistency leads to mistrust.

Temperament is the baby's typical style of responding: easy (regular routines, cheerful), difficult (irregular, intense negative reactions) and slow-to-warm-up (low activity, adjusts slowly to new situations).

example.q: Harlow's monkeys spent most time on the cloth mother and went to the wire mother only to feed. When frightened, they ran to the cloth mother. What does this show?
steps: Feeding alone did not create the bond.
Comfort from soft contact was preferred, especially when afraid.
So attachment depends on contact comfort, not just food.
example.answer: Attachment is based on contact comfort, not just feeding.

topics.title: Childhood: physical growth and Piaget's preoperational and concrete stages

learn.hook: Pour juice from a short, wide glass into a tall, thin one in front of a 4-year-old and she'll say there's 'more juice now'. An 8-year-old will roll her eyes: 'It's the same, you just poured it!'
points: Physical development in childhood is slower than in infancy; gross motor skills (running, jumping) and fine motor skills (writing, buttoning) improve, and handedness becomes established.

Preoperational stage (about 2 to 7 years): symbolic thought appears (using one thing to stand for another, e.g. pretend play with a stick as a horse); thought is egocentric (cannot take another's viewpoint) and shows animism (believing lifeless objects are alive).

Limits of preoperational thought: centration (focusing on one feature, e.g. height of liquid), irreversibility (cannot mentally reverse an action) and lack of conservation; intuitive thought (about 4-7 years) brings many 'why?' questions.

Concrete operational stage (about 7 to 11 years): children understand conservation and reversibility, can classify and seriate (arrange in order by size), and reason logically about concrete objects, but not yet about abstract ideas.
Exam tip: identify the stage from the behaviour described (pretend play/egocentrism → preoperational; conservation/seriation → concrete operational).

example.q: Five-year-old Tara says the moon follows her car, and thinks her teddy feels sad when left alone. Which stage, and which features?
steps: Believing the moon follows her = egocentrism (world centred on her).
Teddy feels sad = animism (lifeless object has feelings).
Both are typical of the preoperational stage.

learn.reallife: When a Class 3 child arranges her pencils from shortest to longest and sorts Diwali sweets by type, she is showing seriation and classification: concrete operational skills.

topics.title: Childhood: self, Erikson's early stages, moral development and influences

learn.hook: A 3-year-old insists, 'I'll pour the water myself!' A 9-year-old proudly shows her science project. Both are working through life stages that Erik Erikson mapped out.
points: In childhood, children form a self-concept (how they describe themselves), learn gender roles (behaviour society expects of boys and girls) and develop self-esteem (how they value themselves).

Erikson's childhood stages: autonomy vs shame and doubt (toddlerhood: doing things oneself), initiative vs guilt (preschool years: planning and trying activities), industry vs inferiority (school years: mastering skills, feeling competent).

Kohlberg's levels of moral reasoning: preconventional (right and wrong judged by rewards and punishments), conventional (following rules, laws and others' approval), postconventional (based on universal ethical principles and personal conscience).
Parents (warm, supportive parenting helps self-esteem) and peers (who teach cooperation, competition and social rules) strongly influence children's development.

example.q: Asked why one shouldn't steal, (a) Raju, 6, says 'You'll get beaten'; (b) Simran, 13, says 'It's against the law and people will think badly of you'; (c) an adult says 'Taking what isn't yours violates others' rights.' Identify Kohlberg's levels.
steps: (a) Focus on punishment → preconventional.
(b) Focus on rules and approval → conventional.
(c) Focus on universal principles → postconventional.

topics.title: Adolescence: puberty, formal operations and egocentrism

learn.hook: One pimple and you're sure the whole class is staring. Feel invincible on a bike without a helmet? Psychologists have names for both feelings, and they are very normal in adolescence.
points: Adolescence is the transition from childhood to adulthood, beginning around puberty and extending into the late teens (roughly 12 to 18-20 years in many accounts).

Puberty brings a growth spurt, the development of secondary sex characteristics (e.g. breasts in girls, facial hair and voice change in boys), and in girls menarche (the first menstruation). Early or late maturation can affect self-image and adjustment differently for boys and girls.

Piaget's formal operational stage (about 11 years onwards): abstract thinking, hypothetical-deductive reasoning (forming and testing hypotheses systematically) and idealism (imagining ideal worlds and comparing reality with them).
Adolescent egocentrism: imaginary audience (believing others are constantly watching and judging you) and personal fable (believing you are unique and invulnerable, 'it won't happen to me').
Adolescents begin to question values and rules; moral reasoning can become more principled.

example.q: Classify: (a) Neha is sure everyone noticed her new haircut and is talking about it; (b) Ravi rides fast without a helmet thinking 'accidents happen to others'; (c) Sana argues about how a perfectly fair society would work.
steps: (a) Belief that others are watching = imaginary audience.
(b) Feeling invulnerable = personal fable.
(c) Thinking about ideal possibilities = idealism (formal operational thought).
example.answer: (a) imaginary audience, (b) personal fable, (c) idealism/formal operational thought

learn.reallife: Debates in school parliaments and Model UN, where teens argue about policies for ideal societies, put formal operational, hypothetical reasoning to work.

learn.hook: 'Science or Arts? Engineer, artist or entrepreneur? Who am I, really?' If these questions keep you up at night, Erikson would say you're doing exactly what adolescents are supposed to do.
points: Erikson's adolescent stage is identity vs role confusion: forming a stable sense of who one is (values, goals, career). Failure leads to confusion about one's roles.
Identity is shaped by family, peers, culture, school and vocational choices; supportive families and opportunities to explore help.

Major concerns: delinquency (law-breaking acts by adolescents), substance abuse (harmful use of alcohol, tobacco or drugs) and eating disorders: anorexia nervosa (severe food restriction with intense fear of weight gain and distorted body image) and bulimia nervosa (episodes of binge eating followed by attempts to prevent weight gain).
These problems are not a sign of weak character; they have psychological, social and biological roots and can be treated. Early help from parents, teachers, counsellors or doctors matters.
Coping and support: healthy routines, talking to trusted people, peer support, counselling and helplines such as Tele-MANAS (14416) help adolescents manage stress.

example.q: Priya, 16, feels confused about her career; her parents want medicine, she loves design. How can she work towards a clear identity?
steps: Identity vs role confusion: she needs to explore options.
Talk openly with parents; try internships or workshops in design and science.
Speak with a school counsellor about interests and aptitude.
Make a choice based on her values and abilities.
example.answer: By exploring options, talking with parents and a counsellor, and choosing based on her values: building identity rather than role confusion.

learn.reallife: Many CBSE schools now have counsellors and wellness teachers, and Tele-MANAS (14416) provides free 24×7 mental-health support in many Indian languages, including for teenagers.

learn.hook: Your parents juggle office deadlines, EMIs and your school fees; your grandparents swap stories of the past. Development keeps posing new challenges long after school ends.
points: Early adulthood: tasks include choosing and settling in a career, marriage, and parenthood. Erikson: intimacy vs isolation, forming close, committed relationships.

Middle adulthood: physical changes (e.g. declining vision); in women, menopause (end of menstruation). Erikson: generativity vs stagnation, contributing to the next generation through work, parenting or mentoring. The 'empty nest' can occur when grown children leave home.

Old age: retirement, physical slowing, some decline in speed of cognitive processing (while knowledge and wisdom may remain), and often widowhood. Erikson: integrity vs despair, looking back on life with satisfaction or regret.
Attitudes to ageing are changing; family support protects against loneliness, while the shift to nuclear families can increase isolation of the elderly.
Activity idea: interview a grandparent about how their life changed from childhood to old age and note the developmental tasks at each stage.

example.q: Mr. Sharma, 68, retired two years ago. He mentors young teachers and feels proud of his life, though he misses his late wife. Which Erikson stage is he in and how is he handling it?
steps: At 68 he is in old age.
Erikson's crisis then is integrity vs despair.
Feeling proud of life and staying engaged shows integrity, though grief is natural.
example.answer: Integrity vs despair; he shows integrity.

learn.reallife: The Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007 and community day-care centres for elders reflect India's response to loneliness and support needs in old age.
